value_or_state_mismatch.content: When selecting an item by an extreme of a fetched metric (e.g., max play_count), don’t predict the winner. Fetch the metric for all candidates (or a sufficient subset), then log a small table of {id, title, metric} and the computed top-1/top-k so the decision is grounded in observed values before taking the downstream action (e.g., play).
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches caused by inventing which record has the highest/lowest metric; makes the decisive per-item fields observable before acting.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: When fetching data, don’t assume the environment will echo the value of the last expression—explicitly `print()`/log key artifacts (e.g., page length, sample item, total accumulated count) and add a clear pagination stop condition (e.g., break when `len(page) < page_limit` or when an explicit `next_page`/`has_more` flag ends) so the observation contains the records you need.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Prevents read/fetch steps from producing uninformative 'Execution successful' observations and avoids infinite/ambiguous pagination loops.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: When doing a read/fetch step, predict the *environment’s* response (returned object shape and/or a snippet of printed content), not a restatement of your code. If you need the observation to include specific fields/text, explicitly `print()` those parts (e.g., `print(resp.keys())`, `print(resp['content'][:N])`) so the run produces inspectable evidence.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Prevents ungrounded expectations where the 'predicted observation' is just code/comments rather than what the environment will actually return or print.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: When logging/printing results of a read/fetch (e.g., Counters or dicts) make sure the object you print is JSON-serializable for the environment: avoid tuple keys or complex objects. Convert keys to strings (e.g., `month_counts_str = {f"{y}-{m:02d}": c for (y,m),c in month_counts.items()}`) or print `list(month_counts.items())` so the observation doesn’t fail.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Prevents losing environment feedback due to print/serialization errors while inspecting fetched metadata.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: After any search/list/paginated fetch that is supposed to produce an object for the next step, explicitly verify it exists before dereferencing (e.g., `if not item: print('not found', page_index, len(page)); ...`) and print minimal diagnostics (page size, a few candidate titles/ids) so you can tell whether the query/pagination found the target before calling detail endpoints.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Prevents wrong-action failures like `NoneType` subscripting and makes it clear whether the read step actually retrieved the needed record.

safe_abstraction.content: In this environment, local Python execution often returns only a generic status (e.g., 'Execution successful.') and does not echo expressions or imports; if you need to observe a value/state for the next step, use explicit output (e.g., print(...) or structured logging) rather than assuming evaluation results will be shown.
safe_abstraction.note: Avoid REPL-style assumptions about local code output; make intermediate values observable when needed.

schema_or_name_mismatch.content: When running multi-statement code blocks, don’t assume the environment will echo the final expression value; explicitly `print(...)` (or otherwise emit) key computed results (counts, samples, booleans) needed for downstream decisions.
schema_or_name_mismatch.note: Some environments only report a generic success message unless values are explicitly printed/emitted, causing apparent schema/output mismatches during local reasoning.

schema_or_name_mismatch.content: Don’t assume printed/returned Python container types will be preserved by the environment (e.g., tuples may serialize as lists). Before downstream use, validate/normalize the in-memory shape you’ll iterate over (e.g., coerce `[(...)]` vs `[[...]]` with `tuple(x)`/`list(x)` or unpack by position) rather than keying logic off the pretty-printed representation.
schema_or_name_mismatch.note: Prevents schema/type surprises caused by environment JSON serialization of local values (tuple->list) during local reasoning.

schema_or_name_mismatch.content: When inspecting local Python dicts via `print(...)`, don’t assume key types are preserved in the displayed output: environments often JSON-serialize results (e.g., int keys become strings). For any downstream logic, rely on the in-memory object (or explicitly normalize with `{int(k): v for k, v in d.items()}` / `{str(k): v ...}`) rather than the printed representation.
schema_or_name_mismatch.note: Prevents schema/type mismatches caused by JSON serialization of printed dicts (key stringification, JSON booleans) during local reasoning.

missing_decisive_information.content: In local reasoning steps, don’t assume the environment will display expression results; explicitly print/return the decisive intermediate values needed for the next action (e.g., list of candidate records, IDs, count, or a small structured preview) so you can verify you selected the right entities before making downstream calls.
missing_decisive_information.note: Some environments only show 'Execution successful' unless you explicitly print; always surface decision-critical intermediates.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When computing a min/max (or other aggregate) over fetched items, validate the result by inspecting a small table of (id, key metric) for several items (or sorting by the metric) to confirm you’re aggregating the intended field across the full set and not skipping items due to missing/None values.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state surprises from unverified local aggregation logic (e.g., min play_count not matching expectations).

value_or_state_mismatch.content: After paginating into an in-memory list, sanity-check that pagination is complete and stable before assuming counts or item order: record how many items each page returns, confirm the last page is empty/short, and inspect a few IDs/titles from the start and end (don’t rely on `items[0]` being a particular object unless the API specifies sorting).
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state surprises caused by incomplete pagination or incorrect assumptions about returned ordering.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When doing batch mutations and reporting summary counts, don’t predict counts from assumptions—record an explicit per-item outcome (e.g., append (id, action_taken, previous_rating) or collect lists for created/updated/skipped/errors) and compute the final totals from those recorded outcomes; optionally sample a few items after the loop to confirm state matches the recorded action.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where printed summaries reflect expectations rather than the actual per-item results of the batch operation.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: Don’t predict concrete counts or example-shaped placeholder records for an in-memory collection that was populated from an API; instead, explicitly inspect `len(items)` and a small, representative sample (e.g., first 3 and last 3 IDs/titles) before basing any downstream logic on assumed size/content.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where the agent acts on imagined list contents or assumed library size rather than the actual fetched state.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When deriving a union/set (e.g., unique IDs aggregated across records), don’t assume the resulting count or members; instead, spot-check the derivation by printing a small per-record breakdown (record_id -> song_ids length + a few IDs) and confirm the union size changes as expected before using the derived set for further logic.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where downstream steps are based on an imagined or unvalidated derived ID set rather than what the fetched records actually contain.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When deriving a target set via intersections/differences (e.g., `A & B`, `A - B`), don’t assume which IDs will be included; print/inspect the immediate inputs (sizes and a few sorted IDs from each set) and, if needed, a small membership table for candidate IDs to confirm the derived membership before using it for downstream actions.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where downstream logic is based on imagined set-intersection membership rather than the actual computed result.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: After building an in-memory mapping from fetched/API-derived data (e.g., `id -> record/tuple`), immediately sanity-check the structure: print a few items plus `type()` of keys and values (and nested fields) to confirm key types (int vs str) and value shape (dict vs tuple/list) match what downstream code expects; normalize (e.g., cast keys to int, standardize value schema) before further filtering/updating.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches caused by silent type/shape drift in locally constructed dicts/lists (e.g., stringified IDs or unexpected list/tuple/dict forms).

value_or_state_mismatch.content: After building an in-memory result list from an API search query, don’t assume the query actually filtered the results: quickly validate relevance by sampling several items and checking that key fields (e.g., title/tags) match the intended constraint; if many don’t, adjust the query (or switch to tag filtering / fetch full items and locally filter) before using counts or selecting candidates.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where downstream steps rely on a search term behaving like a strict filter when the API may return loosely related or unfiltered items.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When a contact search returns multiple results, don’t assume the intended person is the only match. Before using a phone_number, disambiguate by inspecting a compact list of candidates (contact_id, full name, phone_number, email/relationship) and pick the best match (or refine the query) rather than selecting the first/expected record.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents acting on the wrong recipient when search results are broader/noisier than expected.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: Before computing “last N days” windows with `date.today()`/`now()`, first verify the environment’s current date/time (e.g., print `date.today()` or fetch server time) and base your min/max boundaries on that observed value; don’t assume the runtime clock matches real-world/current dates.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches when the execution environment uses a simulated or fixed clock, which would otherwise make time filters silently wrong.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When filtering/joining two in-memory datasets (e.g., transactions filtered by a contacts-derived email set), don’t assume the resulting membership or count. Build a quick validation view: for several candidate records print (record_id, key field, `key in set?`) and also spot-check the set itself (size + a few members). If results are surprising, inspect both sides (e.g., whether a sender email exists in contacts, normalization like lowercasing, and whether the relationship filter returned all intended contacts) before proceeding to mutations.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches caused by unverified local join/filter logic across API-derived datasets.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When using an API “search” endpoint to identify a person/recipient, assume results may be broad or weakly filtered (dozens+ candidates). Always inspect `len(results)` and sample a few entries, then apply a deliberate disambiguation step (e.g., restrict to friends/frequent contacts, match exact email/full name, or intersect with known data like prior transactions) before choosing a single target.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state surprises and wrong-recipient actions caused by treating person search as an exact lookup.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When locally filtering API-derived search results by a predicate like “field is non-null / truthy” (e.g., `friends_since`, `status`, flags), don’t assume it will narrow the list. First compute a quick breakdown (total, count where field is None vs non-None) and sample a few rows showing the field value, then refine the predicate (e.g., exact email/name match, intersect with known prior transactions) before using the filtered set for downstream actions.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state surprises and wrong-recipient choices caused by assuming nullness/truthiness filters are selective without validating the actual distribution in returned results.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When building an in-memory mapping intended to cover a known target set (e.g., person->(name,email)), explicitly validate coverage before proceeding: compare `expected_keys - mapping.keys()` and `mapping.keys() - expected_keys`, and if any are missing, print a short explanation per missing key (e.g., “no matching record found in source list”) and fall back to another lookup path rather than assuming the key exists.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents downstream actions (like creating requests) from silently skipping intended targets due to incomplete locally-derived mappings.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: In environments that often respond with only a generic status (e.g., “Execution successful.”), don’t assume an expression’s value will be shown. If you need to validate a locally-computed dict/list (recipients, payloads, filtered sets), explicitly `print()` it or print a compact summary (len + a few items) before taking any downstream/irreversible action.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where the agent believes it has visually confirmed a local result (recipient selection, request payload) but the environment didn’t actually reveal it.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When an API returns a broad activity feed (e.g., transactions) and you only need records for a specific event, don’t reason from the unfiltered in-memory list. First create and inspect a narrowed subset using explicit filters (query/description match, counterparty email, and/or a date window), then base counts and downstream actions on that subset (print `len(filtered)` and a few sample rows to confirm relevance).
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where the agent assumes the fetched list is already small/relevant and misestimates which items correspond to the current task.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When a people-search endpoint returns unexpectedly large results, first verify the query is actually influencing the output (compare overlap between two different queries; check whether top results contain the query token). If overlap is high or relevance is low, don’t pick from the raw search list—switch to stronger disambiguation (friends-only search, exact email match, or intersect candidates with known counterparties from prior transactions) before choosing recipients.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state surprises and wrong-recipient actions when search endpoints behave like broad directory lookups rather than precise filters.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: Don’t predict concrete values for locally-computed time boundaries or aggregates (e.g., `start_date`, per-recipient totals, grand totals) based on assumptions. Before reporting or making downstream decisions, explicitly inspect the computed intermediates (print the boundary inputs like `date.today()`/computed `start_date`, plus `len()` and a small sample of the per-entity subtotals) so any surprises come from observed state, not imagined placeholders.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where the agent assumes zeros/default dates for aggregates that depend on the environment’s clock and fetched transaction data.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When computing totals by parsing semi-structured text across multiple files/records, don’t assume repeated/constant per-item values. After the loop, explicitly inspect the computed per-item breakdown (e.g., month -> parsed amount) and, if needed, also log what substring/regex match produced each amount before reporting the final aggregate.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where the agent reports imagined uniform subtotals rather than the actually parsed per-file amounts.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: Before acting on a time-based assumption (e.g., “all items are from this month/year” or mapping months to categories), compute and inspect basic timestamp diagnostics from the in-memory list: `len(items)`, `min(date)`, `max(date)`, and a small histogram (e.g., year-month counts). If the distribution differs from expectations, adjust the grouping/filter logic before proceeding to moves/updates.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where downstream organization decisions are based on imagined timestamp distributions rather than observed created_at/updated_at values.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When a file/directory search returns multiple plausible matches (e.g., monthly bills), don’t assume it found the single intended file. First inspect `len(results)` and a short sorted preview, then apply an explicit selection rule (e.g., choose the max by year-month in filename, or filter to the most recent N) before calling `show_file`/parsing.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where downstream logic reads/parses the wrong document because the agent assumed the search would return one canonical match.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When working with an in-memory dict/list that originated from an API response, don’t fill in or assume “typical default” field values (e.g., snooze=0, created_at placeholder). Instead, inspect/print the specific fields you will rely on (or `print(record)` once) and treat missing fields as unknown—only use values you actually observed or explicitly set via an update call.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches caused by mentally substituting expected defaults for API-returned fields.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When you’ve already fetched an object from an API into memory (dict with nested lists), don’t assume placeholder/example values for nested fields (e.g., URLs, titles, IDs). Explicitly `print()`/inspect the real object (or a compact projection like song `(id, title, artist_ids)`) and base downstream selection logic on those observed values.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where the agent reasons from imagined example-shaped content instead of the actual in-memory API result.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: For API-derived items with engagement metrics (e.g., play_count/like_count), don’t assume defaults (like 0) or fabricate example values. Explicitly inspect the metric values (print a small (id,title,metric) table or sort by the metric) before making decisions like “most listened,” and base selections on the observed numbers.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches where the agent predicts placeholder metric values instead of grounding choices in the actual returned counters.

value_or_state_mismatch.content: When you already have an API-returned object in memory (e.g., a dict like `top_song` from `show_song`), don’t predict or restate its non-aggregated fields from schema examples/defaults. If you need specifics (duration, dates, genre, counts, links), explicitly `print()`/inspect the stored object (or re-fetch by id) and treat those concrete values as authoritative for downstream decisions and reporting.
value_or_state_mismatch.note: Prevents value/state mismatches caused by hallucinating placeholder/example field values for data that was actually fetched.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: Don’t rely on bare expression evaluation to reveal in-memory values; explicitly emit the needed details (e.g., `print(var)`, `print(json.dumps(var, indent=2))`, or targeted summaries like counts/keys/samples) so the environment returns actionable content instead of a generic success message.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Local inspection can silently produce non-informative feedback; force explicit output when you need the value for later decisions.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: Before parsing environment-returned date/time strings with strict parsers (e.g., `date.fromisoformat`), first surface the exact string value/format (print it or check a sample) and then parse with the matching `strptime` pattern or a small fallback list of patterns.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Avoid assuming ISO formatting for returned dates; confirm actual format to prevent runtime parse failures in local computations.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: When the sandbox blocks standard helpers (e.g., `io.StringIO`, `open`, `csv.writer`, or similar), don’t keep trying wrappers that depend on those functions. Switch to pure in-memory string construction (manual CSV escaping/quoting) and pass the final string directly to the environment’s file-write API.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Some environments disallow not only file handles but also stdlib convenience functions; treat these restriction errors as a signal to implement minimal formatting manually.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: When inspecting values in this environment, assume `print(...)` may JSON-serialize its arguments; avoid printing objects containing non-serializable types (e.g., datetime/FakeDatetime). Instead print primitive projections (strings/ints) or convert fields first (`dt.isoformat()`, `str(dt)`) before printing or dumping to JSON.
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Prevents inspection-time failures caused by the sandbox print/serialization behavior; print only serializable summaries when debugging local state.

wrong_action_or_failure_mode.content: Assume third-party Python packages may be unavailable in the sandbox. For common tasks (e.g., datetime parsing), prefer stdlib equivalents (`datetime.fromisoformat`, `strptime`) and only add non-stdlib imports after confirming they’re permitted (or be ready with a no-dependency fallback).
wrong_action_or_failure_mode.note: Prevents execution failures from disallowed modules during local reasoning.
